questions.question: Describe the arrangement of a second-class lever using a wheelbarrow, and explain why every second-class lever has a mechanical advantage greater than 1.
questions.expected_answer: In a wheelbarrow the wheel is the pivot, the bricks in the tray are the load and the hands on the handles are the effort, so the load lies between the pivot and the effort. Because the load is always nearer the pivot than the effort, the effort arm is always longer than the load arm, so the effort is always smaller than the load and the mechanical advantage is always greater than 1. The nearer the load is to the wheel, the bigger the advantage.

questions.question: Describe the arrangement of a third-class lever using the human forearm, and explain why a lever with a mechanical advantage below 1 is still useful.
questions.expected_answer: The elbow is the pivot, the biceps pulls on the forearm a few centimetres in front of the elbow as the effort, and the object in the hand is the load at the far end, so the effort lies between the pivot and the load. The effort arm is shorter than the load arm, so the muscle must pull harder than the weight of the load and the mechanical advantage is below 1. It is useful because the load end moves much further and faster than the effort: the lever gives speed, reach and fine control, as in fishing rods, brooms, bats and tweezers.

questions.question: Classify scissors, a nutcracker and tweezers, stating the rule you used, and say which class you would choose for a design that must reverse the direction of a force.
questions.expected_answer: The rule is to ask what lies in the middle. Scissors: pivot in the middle, first class. Nutcracker: load, the nut, in the middle between hinge and hands, second class. Tweezers: effort, the fingers, in the middle between hinge and tips, third class. Only a first-class lever reverses direction, so that class must be chosen when a push on one side must produce movement the other way.
